extracted.intended_audience: policy scholars, administrative law researchers, regulators, and students interested in rulemaking and public comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how administrative agencies respond to organized mass comment campaigns (collections of identical or near-duplicate comments) in rulemaking, using measures of procedural acknowledgement, citation rates, content relevance, and alignment of final regulations with requested changes. Empirical focus in the article is on EPA rulemakings from 2012–2017.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment campaigns are collections of identical and near-duplicate comments sponsored by organizations and submitted by group members and supporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the primary unit of analysis; distinguishes campaign-submitted comments from comments submitted outside campaigns for comparative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural responsiveness (reference in responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how often the agency procedurally references mass comment campaigns in its responses to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by the presence of explicit references to campaigns in agency response documents; the article finds agencies reference campaigns but at lower rates than other comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation rate by comment type
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate at which agencies cite or directly address comments originating from mass campaigns compared to other (non-campaign) comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an empirical proxy for attention or acknowledgement; lower citation rates for campaigns indicate differential procedural treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome consistency (alignment of final rules with requested changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the agency's final regulations are consistent with the specific changes requested in public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess substantive influence of comments; the article reports that regulations are generally not consistent with requested changes, especially for mass comment campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association between campaign participation and regulatory outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The statistical relationship (or lack thereof) between the presence of mass comment campaigns and observed changes in regulatory outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings indicate a lack of association for campaigns relative to other comments, suggesting campaigns have limited substantive effect on rule outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content relevance / presence of 'relevant matter' in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which comments contain issue-specific, substantive information ('relevant matter') that bears on the agency's legal or technical decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article suggests mass comment campaigns generally contain little relevant matter, which helps explain lower substantive responsiveness; implies content quality matters more than comment volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of legal imperatives over political considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which legal requirements and constraints (statutory and evidentiary) condition agency responsiveness, relative to political signals such as mass comment campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an interpretive criterion: observed patterns (low campaign influence) are taken to indicate legal imperatives typically trump political considerations when agencies respond to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical scope and sampling (EPA rulemaking cases/timeframe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope limitation: analysis focuses on 1,049 mass comment campaigns occurring during 22 EPA rulemakings between 2012 and 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the empirical universe for the study and signals that findings are grounded in this sample; useful for assessing generalizability to other agencies, time periods, or rule types.
